danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 11
paragraphs: Midt i denne friske beretning blev Pierre kaldt ind til militærguvernøren.

Da han trådte ind i det private gemak, stod grev Rostoptjin og gned sin pande og sine øjne med hånden med et fortrukkent ansigt. En lille mand var i gang med at sige noget, men da Pierre trådte ind, holdt han op og gik ud.

»Nå, hvordan har De det, store kriger?« sagde Rostoptjin, så snart den lille mand havde forladt rummet. »Vi har hørt om Deres heltedåder. Men det er ikke sagen. Mellem os, mon cher, er De frimurer?« fortsatte han strengt, som om der var noget galt med det, som han ikke desto mindre agtede at tilgive. Pierre tav. »Jeg er velinformeret, min ven, men jeg er klar over, at der er frimurere og frimurere, og jeg håber, at De ikke er en af dem, der under påskud af at redde menneskeheden ønsker at ødelægge Rusland.«
»Ja, jeg er frimurer,« svarede Pierre.

»Ser De, mon cher! Jeg formoder, at De ved, at Speranskij og Magnitskij er blevet deporteret til deres rette plads. Kljutjarev er blevet behandlet på samme måde, og det er andre også, der under påskud af at opbygge Salomons tempel har forsøgt at ødelægge fædrelandets tempel. De kan forstå, at der er grunde til dette, og at jeg ikke kunne have forvist postmesteren, hvis han ikke havde været en skadelig person. Det er nu kommet mig for øre, at De har udlånt ham Deres vogn til hans bortfjernelse fra byen, og at De oven i købet har modtaget papirer fra ham til opbevaring. Jeg kan godt lide Dem og ønsker Dem intet ondt, og — da De kun er halvt så gammel som jeg — råder jeg Dem som en far til at ophøre med al kontakt med folk af den slags og til at rejse herfra så hurtigt som muligt.«
»Men hvad har Kljutjarev gjort forkert, greve?« spurgte Pierre.
»Det er min sag at vide, ikke Deres at spørge om!« råbte Rostoptjin.
»Hvis han er anklaget for at have spredt Napoleons proklamation, er det ikke bevist, at han har gjort det,« sagde Pierre uden at se på Rostoptjin, »og Veresjtjagin...«

»Se, der har vi det!« råbte Rostoptjin til Pierre, endnu højere end før, med en pludselig rynke i panden. »Veresjtjagin er en renegat og en forræder, der vil blive straffet, som han fortjener,« sagde han med den hævngerrige hede, hvormed folk taler, når de erindrer en fornærmelse. »Men jeg har ikke indkaldt Dem for at drøfte mine handlinger, men for at give Dem et råd — eller en ordre, hvis De foretrækker det. Jeg beder Dem om at forlade byen og afbryde al forbindelse med folk som Kljutjarev. Og jeg skal nok banke vrøvlet ud af hvem som helst« — men indså sandsynligvis, at han råbte ad Bezukhov, der hidtil ikke var skyldig i noget, og tilføjede, idet han tog Pierres hånd på en venlig måde: »Vi er på tærsklen til en offentlig katastrofe, og jeg har ikke tid til at være høflig mod alle, der har ærinde hos mig. Mit hoved svimler undertiden. Nå, mon cher, hvad laver De selv personligt?«
»Åh, ingenting,« svarede Pierre uden at hæve blikket eller ændre det tankefulde udtryk i sit ansigt.
Greven rynkede panden.

»Et venskabeligt råd, mon cher. Rejs af sted så hurtigt, De kan, det er alt, jeg har at sige Dem. Lykkelig den, der har øren at høre med. Farvel, min kære ven. Nå, apropos!« råbte han efter Pierre gennem døren, »er det sandt, at grevinden er faldet i kløerne på de hellige fædre i Jesuiterordenen?«
Pierre svarede ikke og forlod Rostoptjins rum mere mut og vred, end han nogensinde før havde vist sig.

Da han nåede hjem, var det allerede ved at blive mørkt. Omkring otte mennesker var kommet for at se ham den aften: sekretæren for et udvalg, obersten for hans bataljon, hans forvalter, hans hovmester og diverse ansøgere. De havde alle ærinde hos Pierre og ville have afgørelser fra ham. Pierre forstod ikke og interesserede sig ikke for nogen af disse spørgsmål og svarede kun på dem for at slippe af med disse mennesker. Da han endelig blev alene, åbnede og læste han sin hustrus brev.

»De, soldaterne ved batteriet, fyrst Andrej dræbt... den gamle mand... Enkelhed er underkastelse under Gud. Lidelse er nødvendig... meningen med alt... man må spænde for... min hustru gifter sig... Man må glemme og forstå...« Og han gik hen til sin seng og kastede sig på den uden at klæde sig af og faldt straks i søvn.

Da han vågnede næste morgen, kom hovmesteren ind for at meddele ham, at et særligt sendebud, en politibetjent, var kommet fra grev Rostoptjin for at høre, om grev Bezukhov var rejst eller var ved at rejse fra byen.
Et dusin mennesker, der havde ærinde hos Pierre, ventede på ham i dagligstuen. Pierre klædte sig hurtigt på og gik i stedet for at tage imod dem ud ad bagtrappen og ud gennem porten.
Fra den tid og til Moskvas ødelæggelses afslutning var der ingen i Bezukhovs husstand, der trods al deres søgen så Pierre igen eller vidste, hvor han var.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: In the middle of this story Pierre was summoned to the commander in chief.

When he entered the private room, Count Rostopchin — his face scrunched up — was rubbing his forehead and eyes with his hand. A short man was saying something, but when Pierre came in, he stopped and left.

"Ah, hello there, great warrior!" said Rostopchin as soon as the short man had gone. "We've heard about your heroics. But that's not why you're here. Between us, my friend — are you a Mason?" He went on sternly, as though there were something wrong with it that he nevertheless intended to overlook. Pierre said nothing. "I am well informed, my friend, but I know there are Masons and Masons, and I hope you are not one of those who, under the pretense of saving mankind, wish to ruin Russia."
"Yes, I am a Mason," Pierre replied.

"There, you see, my friend! I expect you know that Messrs. Speransky and Magnitsky have been sent where they belong. Mr. Klyucharev has been treated the same way, and so have others who, under the guise of building Solomon's Temple, have tried to destroy the temple of their fatherland. You can understand there are reasons for this, and I could not have exiled the Postmaster had he not been a dangerous man. It has now come to my knowledge that you lent him your carriage for his departure from the city, and that you even took papers from him for safekeeping. I like you and don't wish you any harm, and since you're only half my age, I advise you as a father would: cut off all contact with people of that kind and leave here as soon as possible."
"But what did Klyucharev do wrong, Count?" asked Pierre.
"That is for me to know, not for you to ask!" Rostopchin shouted.
"If he is accused of distributing Napoleon's proclamation, it hasn't been proved," said Pierre, not looking at Rostopchin, "and Vereshchagin..."

"There we are!" Rostopchin shouted at Pierre even louder than before, scowling. "Vereshchagin is a renegade and a traitor who will be punished as he deserves," he said with the vindictive heat people show when recalling an insult. "But I didn't summon you to discuss my actions. I summoned you to give you advice — or an order, if you prefer. I ask you to leave the city and sever all ties with people like Klyucharev. And I'll knock the nonsense out of anyone" — but probably realizing he was shouting at Bezukhov, who so far wasn't guilty of anything, he added, taking Pierre's hand in a friendly way — "We're on the eve of a public catastrophe and I haven't time to be polite to everyone who has business with me. My head is spinning sometimes. Well, my friend, what are you doing personally?"
"Nothing," answered Pierre, without raising his eyes or changing his thoughtful expression.
The count frowned.

"A word of friendly advice, mon cher: get out of here as soon as you can — that's all I have to say. Blessed is he who has ears to hear. Goodbye, my dear fellow. Oh, by the way!" he shouted through the doorway after Pierre. "Is it true that the countess has fallen into the clutches of the holy fathers of the Society of Jesus?"
Pierre did not answer and left Rostopchin's room more sullen and angry than he had ever shown himself.

When he reached home it was already getting dark. About eight people had come to see him that evening: the secretary of a committee, the colonel of his battalion, his steward, his major-domo, and various petitioners. They all had business with Pierre and needed decisions. Pierre didn't understand any of their questions and wasn't interested in them; he answered only to get rid of these people. When finally left alone, he opened and read his wife's letter.

"They — the soldiers at the battery, Prince Andrew killed... that old man... Simplicity is submission to God. Suffering is necessary... the meaning of everything... one must harness... my wife is getting married... One must forget and understand..." And going to his bed he threw himself on it without undressing and instantly fell asleep.

When he woke the next morning, the major-domo came to tell him that a special messenger — a police officer — had come from Count Rostopchin to find out whether Count Bezukhov had left or was leaving the city.
A dozen people with business were waiting for Pierre in the drawing room. He dressed hurriedly and, instead of going to see them, went to the back porch and out through the gate.
From that time until the end of Moscow's destruction, none of the Bezukhov household — despite all their searching — saw Pierre again or knew where he was.
